justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assumed was a recent market price around 294–295, with each successive horizon incorporating a small positive drift assumption. For the one-day horizon, the estimate of 295.5 essentially assumes very little movement from the prior close, consistent with the typical daily volatility of a broad equity index or similar instrument and the absence of any imminent scheduled catalyst that would force a directional view. The one-week estimate of 296.5 adds a slightly larger drift, reflecting a baseline assumption that equity markets tend to trend modestly upward over short horizons in the absence of negative shocks. The one-month estimate of 298.0 extends this logic further, incorporating a small annualized return assumption of roughly 5–8% which, when compressed to a single month, produces only a modest nominal gain above current levels.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated using typical realized volatility for broad equity indices, which tends to run in the range of 12–18% annualized. At one day, this translates to a relatively tight band of roughly plus or minus 8–9 points around the point estimate. At one week, the interval widens to roughly plus or minus 16–17 points, scaling with the square root of time. At one month, the interval expands to roughly plus or minus 33–34 points, reflecting the accumulation of daily uncertainties over approximately 21 trading days. These widths also incorporate a small additional buffer for parameter uncertainty and the possibility of volatility regimes shifting during the forecast horizon.

There are meaningful tail risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data, an unexpected central bank policy shift toward aggressive tightening, or a geopolitical shock could produce sharp drawdowns that breach the lower bound of even the one-day interval in extreme scenarios. Credit market stress or a liquidity event could amplify moves significantly. On the upside, a strong positive surprise in earnings, inflation data coming in well below expectations, or a dovish pivot signal from a major central bank could drive prices above the upper bounds, particularly at the one-week and one-month horizons where the intervals are already wider.

Finally, it is worth acknowledging that my estimates were made without access to real-time market data, so the actual prevailing price at forecast time may differ from my assumed starting point, which would shift all estimates and intervals accordingly. Model risk is also present: if the true data-generating process has fat tails, heavier than normal kurtosis, or is subject to jump diffusion dynamics, then my normally-distributed confidence intervals will systematically understate the probability of extreme outcomes. In practice, roughly 10–15% of financial return distributions in monthly windows exhibit tail events
